title: Getting GDPR ready
intro: Seven stages, from a fresh install to being able to show a regulator your records. You do not have to follow the order. A stage turns green when everything in it is done or marked as not applying to you. GDPR is about your data, so most of the work is writing down what personal data you have, why, and who looks after it.

stages.name: Set the product up
stages.aim: Get the tool ready and the right people into it. About an hour.

tasks.title: Add the people who will keep the records
tasks.do: Go to Users and add the people who own personal data in each department: HR, sales, marketing, IT, finance. Give each the smallest role that lets them do their job.
tasks.why: GDPR records go out of date when one person keeps them alone. The people who use the data know it best.

tasks.title: Turn on email
tasks.do: In Settings, put in your mail server details and send yourself a test message.
tasks.why: Reminders are how owners hear that a request is due, a breach clock is running, or an entry needs its yearly review.

tasks.title: Put your logo on reports
tasks.do: In Reports, upload your organisation's logo.
tasks.why: The accountability report may go to a regulator. It should carry your name.

tasks.title: Keep a copy of the backup somewhere else
tasks.do: A backup runs every night. Open Backups, press Download on the newest one, and keep that file somewhere other than this server.
tasks.why: These records are your proof of compliance. A backup on the same machine protects you from very little.

stages.name: Map your personal data
stages.aim: Write down every way you use personal data. This is the data map (Article 30), and everything else builds on it.

tasks.title: Add your first entries to the data map
tasks.do: Open Data map. Use the Templates tab to add common activities like payroll, customer orders or CCTV, or the Questionnaire tab to go department by department.
tasks.why: You cannot protect, explain or delete data you do not know you have.

tasks.title: Ask every department what data it uses
tasks.do: Sit with each department head and go through the Questionnaire tab for their department. Add anything that is not in the list.
tasks.why: The data map is only as good as the departments' answers. Teams often use spreadsheets and apps that IT does not know about.

tasks.title: List the systems that hold personal data
tasks.do: In Assets, add each system, app and paper file that holds personal data: the HR system, the CRM, the shared drive, the filing cabinet. The Sample library tab has common ones.
tasks.why: The data map says why you use data; the asset list says where it is. You need both to answer a request or contain a breach.

tasks.title: Choose a lawful basis for every entry
tasks.do: Open each data map entry and pick one of the six lawful bases. If it is legitimate interests, write down why in the notes.
tasks.why: Article 6: using personal data without a lawful basis is unlawful, however careful you are with it.

tasks.title: Give every entry an owner
tasks.do: Put a named owner and their email on every entry. They will get a reminder when it is due for its yearly review.
tasks.why: A record with no owner is never reviewed, and an old record is a wrong record.

stages.name: Tell people what you do
stages.aim: People have a right to know how you use their data (Articles 12 to 14), and consent must be provable (Article 7).

tasks.title: Publish a privacy notice
tasks.do: Write a privacy notice for each group: customers, staff, website visitors. Add each under Notices and policies with the kind 'Privacy notice', and mark it Approved.
tasks.why: The notice must match your data map. A regulator reads the two side by side.

tasks.title: Record how you collect consent
tasks.do: For every place you ask for consent (a sign-up form, a cookie banner), add a consent record with the wording and a screenshot.
tasks.why: If you rely on consent you must be able to prove it was given, and show how people can take it back.

stages.name: Check the risky parts
stages.aim: Some uses of data can seriously affect people. Those need an impact assessment before they start (Article 35).

tasks.title: Decide which entries are high risk
tasks.do: On each data map entry, set 'High risk?' to Yes or No. If unsure, open DPIAs, start one, and answer the screening questions.
tasks.why: Large-scale, sensitive, monitoring or automated processing usually needs a DPIA. The screening tells you.

tasks.title: Complete a DPIA for each high-risk entry
tasks.do: In DPIAs, link one to each high-risk entry, score the risks, write down what you will do about them, and get it approved.
tasks.why: Starting high-risk processing without a DPIA is itself a breach of GDPR.

stages.name: Sort out your suppliers
stages.aim: Anyone who handles personal data for you needs a contract (Article 28), and data leaving the EU needs protection (Articles 44 to 49).

tasks.title: List the suppliers who handle personal data
tasks.do: In Processors and suppliers, add every supplier that stores or sees personal data for you: payroll, cloud, email, CRM.
tasks.why: You are responsible for what your processors do with your data.

tasks.title: Get a signed DPA from each processor
tasks.do: Upload the signed data processing agreement (DPA) on each supplier and set the DPA status to Signed.
tasks.why: Article 28 requires a written contract with set terms. Most big suppliers publish one you can accept.

tasks.title: Cover every transfer outside the EU
tasks.do: On each supplier, say whether data leaves the EU, to which countries, and what covers it, for example standard contractual clauses.
tasks.why: A transfer with nothing to cover it is one of the most common GDPR fines.

stages.name: Be ready for requests and breaches
stages.aim: Requests from people have a one-month deadline, and breaches a 72-hour one. Be ready before the first one arrives.

tasks.title: Agree who handles requests from individuals
tasks.do: Decide who receives access, erasure and other requests, how identity is checked, and how all of a person's data is found. Log every request in Requests.
tasks.why: One month goes quickly when nobody knows whose job it is.

tasks.title: Agree how a breach is reported inside the organisation
tasks.do: Tell staff who to call when data is lost, sent to the wrong person, or hacked. Log every breach in Breaches, even small ones.
tasks.why: The 72 hours start when the organisation becomes aware, not when the right person hears about it.

tasks.title: Decide whether you need a Data Protection Officer
tasks.do: Check Article 37. Write down your decision and the reason, and attach it as evidence on that duty.
tasks.why: Public bodies and organisations that monitor people or handle sensitive data at scale must appoint one.

stages.name: Keep it true, and prove it
stages.aim: Accountability (Article 5(2)) means being able to show your records at any time.

tasks.title: Give every GDPR duty an owner
tasks.do: Open Duties, give each one an owner, and mark how far along it is.
tasks.why: It turns the law into a list of named jobs.

tasks.title: Attach proof
tasks.do: Upload policies, training records and other documents in Evidence, and link each to the duty it proves.
tasks.why: A regulator wants to see documents, not hear promises.

tasks.title: Review the data map every year
tasks.do: Each owner gets a reminder 12 months after the last review. Open the entry, check it is still right, and set Last reviewed to today.
tasks.why: Data maps go out of date quickly. A yearly review keeps them true.

tasks.title: Export the accountability report
tasks.do: In Reports, download the Accountability report. Keep a copy, and send it when a regulator or customer asks.
tasks.why: It puts the data map, DPIAs, requests, breaches, processors and consent in one document.

tasks.title: Report to management once a year
tasks.do: Once a year, take the accountability report to management. Agree what needs fixing, and add each fix as a task with an owner and a date.
tasks.why: GDPR makes the organisation responsible, not one person. Management needs to see the state of things and back the fixes.
